Released by Blackhawk Films, "The Coming of the Streamliners" uses newsreel footage to show the dramatic rise of streamlined railroad technology during the early 20th century, beginning with the introduction of America’s first bullet train—a lightweight, diesel-driven marvel capable of 110 miles per hour that promised to revolutionize rail travel and industry. This innovation leads to the development of other famous trains such as the Zephyr, which thrilled passengers on record-breaking runs between Denver and Chicago, and the sleek Super Chief that cut cross-country travel time to a day and a half. Around the world, similar advances appeared: France’s aerodynamic express between Paris and La Rochelle, Germany’s two-story double-decker train, and Canada’s enormous streamline locomotive celebrating a century of rail service. The era culminates with the Silver Meteor at the New York World’s Fair, symbolizing luxury and modernity in motion. However, the optimism of technological progress ends darkly with news of a deliberate train wreck in Nevada—a grim reminder that even the triumphs of speed and innovation could not escape the dangers of human malice.

The railroad industry's focus on improved speed and power.0:41 - 1934: The first American bullet train is presented and accepted by Mr. Harriman, signaling the start of a new era in rail travel.0:49 - This technological advancement is expected to be available to all U.S. railroads, potentially replacing old equipment nationwide.1:06 - It is described as a major boost for industrial recovery and economic progress.1:18 - The streamlined, diesel-driven train can reach 110 mph, halving travel time between Chicago and Los Angeles and offering luxury with air-conditioned, shatterproof coaches.1:38 - Built of lightweight duralumin, the three-car train weighs as much as one Pullman car, representing beauty, speed, and progress—a “new deal” for railroads. 2:01 -Las Vegas, Nevada: the bullet train visits Boulder Dam, a marvel of modern engineering, before the dam’s reservoir submerges nearby approaches.2:59  Philadelphia, 1934: The Zephyr train makes its trial run, reaching 107 mph, thrilling passengers as the landscape blurs past.3:26 - Dubbed the “Zephyr Cyclone,” it outpaces an airplane and will soon serve routes between Kansas City, Omaha, and Lincoln.3:47 -Streamline Zephyr makes record run between Denver and Chicago. The Zephyr’s oil-powered efficiency cuts operating costs by two-thirds, marking a leap in railroad progress.4:10 - 1934. France unveils its own streamlined train between Paris and La Rochelle, reaching 90 mph, matching the city’s fast-paced spirit.7:13 - 1936. Germany introduces a two-story double-decker train seating 300 passengers, cutting travel time in half between Lübeck and Hamburg.7:46 - 1936. The Super Chief, a lightweight 3,600-horsepower diesel train, makes its first run from Chicago to Los Angeles in just 36 hours, reaching speeds up to 100 mph.10:45 - 1939. This silent black-and-white home movie from 1939 follows a husband and wife, possibly Drs. Irene and Lloyd C. Shanklin, who billed themselves as expert biochemists and food scientists but were probably quacks. The couple were the owners of Harmony Health Center aka Shanklin Groves of Homestead, Florida. The film begins with odd footage of the couple demonstrating the uses of aloe vera as a moisturizer. They then travel to Washington, D.C., where the footage captures prominent landmarks of the capital. Later, they visit a resort, followed by scenes of various structures, some under construction, resembling Egyptian-inspired architecture. The film concludes with the couple back at Harmony Health, where they pick fruits and showcase an abundant harvest of crops, fruit trees, and plants. (Note: in 1959 Lloyd Shanklin was charged with making false claims about a preparation made of aloe leaves and papaya rica.)

This film "Weight Training" (part 1)  was produced by Dr. Frank Ryan and Ryan Films in 1963, and was part of a series of physical conditioning educational films produced by the company.  It shows a bodybuilder using weights as part of a physical fitness regimen, and shows how this type of conditioning is important for various careers including working construction. Expresses the opinion that much of the athletic achievement in recent years has been due to weight training and indicates the events associated with weight training or weight lifting. The part played by the various muscles in these events are pointed out, and the training program for developing these muscles illustrated and described. Dr. Francis Joseph Ryan became well known for his knowledge relating to sports training. 

00:00 Main titles. Introduction and Physiology 0:43 — The Age of Achievement: The film attributes modern athletic record-breaking to the rise of weight training.
 1:08 — Muscle Mechanics: Explains that all movement depends on muscle contraction. It uses the arm and leg as examples of hinge joints moved by the shortening of muscle fibers (biceps for flexion, quadriceps for extension).
 1:54 — Progressive Resistance: Defines weight training as the body adjusting to work. Its two main advantages are precise measurement of resistance and the ability to target specific muscles.
Competitive and Basic Lifts 2:25 — Olympic Weightlifting: Demonstrates the three international lifts: the Two-Arm Press, the Two-Arm Snatch, and the Two-Arm Clean and Jerk.
 3:33 — The Importance of Warm-up: Stresses that all workouts must begin with a warm-up to saturate muscles with blood, reducing soreness and the risk of injury.
 3:52 — Upper Body Basics:
 The Press: Primarily targets the triceps.
 The Curl: Develops the biceps and forearms.
 The Bench Press: Targets triceps and shoulders; a narrow grip emphasizes the triceps.
Targeting Specific Muscle Groups 5:40 — Shoulders (Deltoids): Discusses the three parts of the deltoid muscle. Exercises include dumbbell lateral raises (sideways), forward raises, and bent-over lateral raises.
 6:45 — Chest (Pectorals):  Straight Arm Pullover: Used to increase the size of the rib cage (utilizing light weights for leverage).
 Lateral Raises Lying: Direct pectoral development.
 7:43 — Back (Latissimus Dorsi & Trapezius):  Bent-over Rowing: Targets the "lats."
 Upright Rowing: Targets the trapezius and deltoids.
 Shoulder Shrugs: Specifically for the trapezius.
 8:54 — Abdominals and Obliques:
 Side Bending: Strengthens the external obliques.
 Sit-ups and V-ups: Strengthen the rectus abdominis. Progress is made by holding weights behind the neck.
Lower Body and Back Development 10:06 — The Squat (Knee Bend): Called the most valuable exercise for thigh and hip power. The film recommends partial squats (thighs parallel to the ground) to avoid knee strain.
 11:24 — Isolation Leg Work:  Leg Curls: Using "iron boots" to target the hamstrings.
 Leg Extensions: Directly exercising the quadriceps.
 12:13 — Lower Back and Calves:
 Deadlift: Develops the erector spinae (lower back). Requires bent knees and a straight back for safety.
 Heel Raise: Develops the calves; using a board allows for a full range of flexion.
Variations and Conclusion 13:17 — Grip and Position Variations:  Reverse Curls: Palms down to target forearms.
 Wide Grip Bench Press: Increases pectoral involvement.
 Press Behind Neck: Involves the deltoids more than a standard press.
 Hack Lift: A behind-the-back squat that also develops grip strength.
 15:00 — Summary: The film concludes that a well-planned program—starting with light weights and progressing to heavier ones—is essential for any athlete to reach their full potential.

Produced by Monumental Films for the Portland Cement Association, "The Dual Purpose Room" (1961) was designed to familiarize contractors with fallout shelter construction.This Cold War-era civil defense film follows the fictional Jones family as they decide to build a fallout shelter after learning about the dangers of radioactive fallout from nuclear weapons. Through conversations, government guidance, and a step-by-step construction demonstration, the film explains shelter design, radiation protection, required emergency supplies, and preparedness measures. It promotes concrete masonry fallout shelters as practical dual-purpose family spaces while encouraging citizens to take an active role in civil defense planning and emergency readiness.

00:00– An average suburban family is introduced as John Jones presents his wife Mary, son Tommy, and their comfortable home life.1:03 – During a typical evening, Mary announces she wants to discuss something important after Tommy goes to bed.1:44 – Mary raises concerns about radioactive fallout and insists the family should build a fallout shelter.2:42 – Despite John's objections over cost and his savings for an outboard motor, Mary argues that a shelter is necessary for family safety.3:16 – Mary shares information from a civil defense presentation explaining the dangers of radioactive fallout after a nuclear attack.3:54 – A cartoon within the film explains how fallout particles emit harmful radiation and why sheltering behind thick materials offers protection.4:56 – Convinced by the evidence and his wife's determination, John agrees to build a shelter.5:18 – The family consults a masonry contractor who is already familiar with government shelter plans.5:51 – The contractor explains that concrete block shelters can be attractive, economical, and serve as multipurpose rooms.6:29 – Government programs encouraging shelter construction are highlighted, along with alternative shelter designs for homes without basements.7:06 – Construction begins as the contractor lays out the shelter walls and starts building with concrete masonry units.8:18 – The film demonstrates proper masonry techniques, including alignment, mortar application, and level checks.9:09 – Hollow blocks are filled with sand for added protection, and the shelter walls are completed.9:30 – Roof beams, protective ceiling layers, and a radiation-shielding baffle wall are installed.9:57 – The completed shelter is painted and furnished as a comfortable dual-purpose family room.10:32 – Civil defense director Leo Hoegh inspects the shelter and explains its protective design features.11:19 – Essential shelter supplies are reviewed, including food, water, medical supplies, batteries, and emergency equipment.11:58 – The film stresses personal preparedness and outlines five civil defense essentials for every American family.13:24 – The Jones family receives a certificate from the Office of Civil Defense and Mobilization. The family settles into their finished shelter, and John concludes that protecting his family was worth sacrificing his outboard motor.

Dating to 1928, this silent Eastman Classroom Film "Purifying Water" was supervised by August Oddleifson. The film shows the modern water system in Chicago, which purifies water for the city from Lake Michigan by using natural filtration and chlorine. At 0:00 main titles followed by shots of fountains in Chicago. At 0:25,  the Four Mile Crib Lighthouse on Lake Michigan is shown. The structure houses and protects offshore water intakes used to supply the city with drinking water. The Four Mile Crib was built in 1891 and is located four miles offshore from the foot of Chicago's 14th Street. A diagram at 0:34 explains this. At 1:01 the Gothic Revival style Chicago Avenue Pumping Station on Michigan Avenue, designed by William Boyington. At 1:50, settling tanks are used to remove sediment from water. At 2:29, chemicals may be added to hasten settling. 3:19 water is filtered through sand and gravel, and a demonstration of how this works is shown.  At 5:34, a water treatment plant is shown. At 6:41, title card: The flow of water may be reversed to clean the filter beds. 7:28: title card: water may contain harmful bacteria. A diagram shows how fresh water supplies can be contaminated by sewage or other dirty water.  9:19: a chlorine treatment facility is shown, with chlorine injected into city water supplies. 10:49: title card: water is tested daily. Testing is shown using petrie dishes in a laboratory, which are stored for 24 hours to see if there is bacterial growth. The End.

This film by Ron Harris "Circus Comes to Town" (1946) shows the Belle Vue Circus in Manchester, UK. It starts with music and the orchestra playing as attendants move towards the ring. The ringmaster (probably the famous George Lockhart) ensures everything is in order, and the first night begins with an Indian bareback rider escorted by clowns. The rider, known as the great white Chief Running Water, demonstrates his horsemanship, followed by a performance from the famous three Austin clowns. The conductor cues the next act, a hand balancer, who performs impressive balancing tricks. The Shetland ponies, with their lady trainer, respond to orders and perform well. The trapeze artists, including the flying twins, perform daring stunts, such as the human pendulum. The famous Adagio dancers, Bol and Merin, perform, with the girl jumping from a high platform and being caught safely by her partner. The clowns return with comedic stunts, followed by a knife thrower, the merry muttons Mavis and Mmadu, a strongman act, a wire walker, and a juggler performing with rings. The Oxfords then perform a basketball game on bikes, which continues with fast-paced action. The audience rises as the first night ends with the playing of the king.

The first Belle Vue Circus (so named because it took place at the eponymous Belle Vue Gardens) took place in 1922, and again in 1929. After that year it became a regular Christmas-time event held in the Kings Hall. Ringmaster George Lockhart became synonymous with the Belle Vue Circus, and his face was used on many advertising posters. Belle Vue Zoo superintendent Gerald Iles included some of the zoo's animals in the circus, in a feature called Noah's Ark. Another of the circus stalwarts was resident band leader and Belle Vue's musical director Fred Bonelli, who led various Belle Vue circus bands for 40 years, and  Jacko the Clown and his partner "Little Billy" Merchant, who performed for three decades. The last circus to take place in the Kings Hall before its sale was in 1981.

This reel of silent, color home movie footage was captured circa 1962 by an unknown American filmmaker prior to American involvement in the Vietnam War. It begins with an Army of the Republic of Vietnam (ARVN) military demonstration at an outdoor soccer stadium, possibly Cộng Hoà Stadium (now Thống Nhất Stadium). It then shows scenes shot in more rural areas, including shots of a junk or sampan fishing fleet. The location is unknown but might be Vung Tau or Cap Saint-Jacques, both popular retreats from Saigon during the war. A large hotel is visible at (14:11) but has so far been unidentified. 

0:00 The film opens with armed female AVRN members practicing for a drill or demonstration in an outdoor stadium (:10). They pass empty stands soon to be filled for a formal review (1:08). Women hold rifles in the center of the greenway (1:23). Shots sweep military trucks, large barrels and ammunition supplies (1:37). Close angles watch the female soldiers march (2:07). The stands and field fill for the formal drill (2:26). An official stands at the podium (2:55). Crowds line the sidelines (3:08). A group of young soldiers walk off the grounds; Southern Vietnamese flags wave at the bottom screen (3:35). A medic truck sits outside the arena (3:43). Footage transitions to a man in a wooded area (7:02) springing up a tree. Ropes hang from the trees (7:24). At the top of the tree he balances a large stick as telephone wires hang in the background (7:30). He slips to the ground using the ropes (7:54) dropping into attention barefoot on the dirt (8:01). Two locals row a small boat over blue waters; one wears a rice paddy hat (8:03). Junk boats fill the harbor (8:14). Footage sweeps an open air market (8:31). Locals move goods and supplies on and off boats (8:42). Numerous sampans fill harbor waters, mountains rim the background (9:34). The flat bottomed boats are iconic of Vietnam used for transportation, fishing as well as for military transport during the war. Footage switches to the fishing village, women fix one another’s hair seated on the ground by a bamboo fence (10:00). Four children pose happily together (10:11). Shots pan over thatched roof dwellings for a pile of sandbags and a lookout post or observation tower (10:28). Footage continues to move over the bamboo exterior wall (10:53). A group huddles over a gameboard (11:00). Another carts a large portion of fishing net using carrying pole (11:51). The iconic thung chair boat; a round basket boat often used by fishermen, appears (12:08). Close shots watch a man’s hand sew a fishing net (12:25). In the background at (14:11), a large resort hotel is visible. A pair smoke tobacco at an outdoor table littered with booze bottles (14:24). The film concludes with images of locals passing uniformed military men of the AVRN (14:51) as well as Southern Vietnamese National Police in white uniforms (15:00) in an unidentified town.
